title: Supplies
description: Qualified supplies are tangible, non-depreciable property, such as raw materials and reagents, used directly in qualified research under IRC Section 41.
summary: Qualified supplies are tangible, non-depreciable property—such as raw materials, reagents, and pilot model components—used directly in qualified research, counting as in-house qualified research expenses under IRC Section 41 for U.S. taxpayers. Land, improvements to land, depreciable equipment, leased property, and general overhead are excluded, and taxpayers must substantiate and report supply costs by business component on Form 6765.

body.text: Qualified supplies are tangible, non-depreciable property—such as raw materials, reagents, and pilot model components—used directly in qualified research, counting as in-house qualified research expenses under IRC Section 41 for U.S. taxpayers. Land, improvements to land, depreciable equipment, leased property, and general overhead are excluded, and taxpayers must substantiate and report supply costs by business component on Form 6765.
Executive Summary and Core Legal Corrections

Supplies constitute a foundational statutory category of in-house Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), operating alongside employee wages for qualified services, eligible computer time-sharing expenditures, and third-party contract research expenses. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C), a taxpayer carrying on a trade or business may claim amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, where the statute defines supplies strictly as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1) enforces a stringent operational nexus: eligible supplies must be used directly in the performance of qualified services by an employee of the taxpayer (or a person acting in a similar capacity), which categorically excludes indirect research expenditures and general and administrative (G&A) overhead.

A comprehensive audit of standard tax compliance frameworks governing Section 41 supply claims against primary statutory text, Treasury Regulations, United States Tax Court precedent, and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) administrative guidance confirms the overarching mechanics of the credit while establishing five critical legal and technical corrections required for defensible tax positions.

First, regarding the statutory versus regulatory origin of the tangibility and depreciation rules, secondary tax commentary frequently attributes the "tangible personal property" requirement and the exclusions for land and depreciable property to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2. In law, the tangibility mandate and the exclusions for land, improvements to land, and depreciable property are codified directly in the statute at 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(i)–(ii), which employs the exact statutory phrase "any tangible property" rather than the paraphrased formulation "tangible personal property".

Second, regarding the 80% "Substantially-All" Rule on prototype materials, practitioners frequently misstate that if 80% or more of the total monetary costs incurred in building a prototype are attributable to a process of experimentation, the "Substantially-All Rule" converts 100% of the prototype's material costs—including minor non-experimental production costs—into qualified supplies. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the 80% "substantially all" rule actually measures whether 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation. It does not apply to prototype material purchase prices, nor does it override 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) or IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), which strictly bar production costs paid or incurred after technical uncertainty is eliminated.

Third, regarding the legal standard for depreciability versus physical consumption and financial accounting labels, compliance guides often assert that financial accounting expensing is a direct determinant of tax eligibility and that only physically consumed or destroyed items can qualify as supplies. Under United States Tax Court precedent in T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), physical destruction or exhaustion is not a statutory prerequisite. Rather, eligibility turns on whether the tangible property is subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167 in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit, and financial accounting labels on a taxpayer's general ledger are never controlling for federal income tax purposes.

Fourth, regarding the IRS examination posture on supply QRE proportions, while industry benchmarks in physical manufacturing often model supplies as representing 15% to 20% of total QREs (alongside approximately 70% for wages and 10% to 15% for contract research), the official IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG): Qualified Research Expenses (last updated July 2, 2026) explicitly instructs examiners that supply QREs, in general, should represent a small portion of total QREs. When claimed supply QREs are substantial, IRS examiners are directed to flag the return for the potential inclusion of capital assets or ineligible overhead expenses.

Fifth, regarding upfront project-level disclosure on redesigned Form 6765, compliance extends well beyond general record retention under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d). The redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) and Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) require taxpayers to report supply costs by individual business component in Section G (Column 54) and in summary on Section F (Line 43)—a reporting regime that is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return claiming or increasing a research credit) and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025.
Statutory and Regulatory Pillars of Supplies QREs
The Legal Foundation and In-House Research Categories

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), a taxpayer's total Qualified Research Expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer consist of the sum of two overarching statutory categories: in-house research expenses under § 41(b)(1)(A) and contract research expenses under § 41(b)(1)(B). Although general tax summaries frequently describe employee wages, supplies, and contract research as the three pillars of QREs, the statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A) actually enumerates three distinct subcategories within in-house research expenses alone.

First, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) encompasses any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee. Second, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) covers any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. Third, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), as implemented by 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4), covers amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research, provided that the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, is located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user of the computer.

Separately from in-house research expenses, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1) define contract research expenses as 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research performed on behalf of the taxpayer. Specific statutory exceptions increase this allowable percentage from 65% to 75% for amounts paid or incurred to a qualified scientific research consortium under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(C), and to 100% for eligible energy research payments made to eligible small businesses, institutions of higher education, or federal laboratories under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D).
The Direct Nexus Requirement to Qualified Services

Claiming a material expenditure under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) requires affirmative proof that the supply was "used in the conduct of qualified research". Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1) establishes the controlling operational standard for this functional nexus: supplies are used in the conduct of qualified research only if they are used in the performance of qualified services (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof) by an employee of the taxpayer, or by a person acting in a capacity similar to that of an employee of the taxpayer. As illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(5), Example 6, a person acting in a capacity similar to an employee includes contracted temporary laboratory personnel working under the taxpayer's supervision.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i)–(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), "qualified services" are strictly limited to three functional tiers of activity. The first tier is engaging in qualified research, which denotes the actual, hands-on conduct of experimental activities by scientists, engineers, or laboratory technicians executing trials or fabricating experimental models. The second tier is the direct supervision of qualified research, which covers first-line management directly supervising the technical personnel conducting the experimentation, but excludes higher-level executives or multi-tier managers to whom those first-line supervisors report. The third tier is the direct support of qualified research, which encompasses hands-on operational support essential to either the researchers engaging in experimentation or their first-line supervisors. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) and Footnote 6 of the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses, direct support includes a machinist machining a part for an experimental model used in qualified research, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data, or a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research.

A critical second-order compliance rule emerges from the explicit regulatory carve-out in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1), which mandates that supplies must be used in the performance of qualified services "as defined in section 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof". The final sentence of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)—implemented for wage QREs by 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)—contains the "substantially all" rule for employee compensation, under which 100% of an employee's annual wages qualify if at least 80% of that employee's total services during the taxable year consist of qualified services. By expressly severing that sentence from 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1), the Treasury Regulations prohibit taxpayers from claiming 100% of the tangible materials consumed by an "80%+ qualified" research engineer if a portion of those materials was actually consumed during the non-qualifying 20% of the engineer's duties (such as commercial production trouble-shooting or routine quality control). Every claimed supply expenditure must independently satisfy the direct nexus test without piggybacking on an employee's 80% wage qualification threshold.
Tangibility, the Depreciation Bar, and the Consumption Standard

The threshold definition of a qualified supply is codified directly in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), which provides that the term "supplies" means any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. While secondary accounting literature frequently paraphrases this requirement as "tangible personal property," both 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) and the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses apply the exact statutory formulation "any tangible property".

This statutory architecture imposes three mandatory legal gates that an expenditure must clear before its functional use in research is even evaluated. Under Gate 1 (Tangibility), the expenditure must acquire physical, tangible property. Intangible expenditures and service fees—including software licenses, patent application attorney fees, royalties, professional association dues, telephone or internet communications charges, travel, meals, entertainment, employee relocation expenses, and equipment or facility lease payments—are categorically barred from qualifying as supplies because they do not constitute tangible property. While legal fees for procuring a patent may qualify as research or experimental expenditures under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Activities underscores that IRC Section 41 is substantially narrower than IRC Section 174 and unconditionally disallows patent legal fees as QREs.

Under Gate 2 (Real Property Exclusion, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(i)), land and improvements to land—encompassing buildings, structural foundations, cleanroom structural build-outs, permanent facility fixtures, and real estate acquisition or improvement costs—are statutorily excluded from supplies.

Under Gate 3 (The Depreciation Bar, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii)), property "of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" is unconditionally excluded from supply QREs. Whether tangible property is of a character subject to depreciation for purposes of IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) is determined by reference to IRC § 167, which governs property used in a trade or business or held for the production of income that possesses a useful life extending beyond the taxable year and is subject to wear and tear, exhaustion, or obsolescence. Furthermore, although annual depreciation allowances on capital equipment used in research may in specific circumstances be treated as research expenditures under IRC § 174 (pursuant to 26 CFR § 1.174-2(b)(1)), the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Activities states unequivocally that depreciation itself is never a QRE under IRC Section 41.

A vital legal distinction governs the interplay between the statutory depreciation bar, physical consumption, and financial accounting treatment. Although physical consumption, permanent alteration, or destruction during testing—such as chemical reagents, 3D printing filament, exotic metal alloys, and disposable laboratory glassware—is the most frequent practical indicator that an item lacks a lasting useful life and is non-depreciable, the United States Tax Court in T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), expressly rejected the IRS's administrative position that supplies must be physically used up or exhausted. Similarly, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) confirms that the ultimate sale or use of tangible property resulting from research is irrelevant to its Section 174 eligibility. The controlling legal question under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) is strictly whether the tangible property is subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167 in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit. Conversely, as the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses warns, "Taxpayer labels are not controlling": expensing a capital machine on the general ledger under a financial accounting de minimis policy does not transform that asset into a qualified supply if the property is legally of a character subject to depreciation under IRC § 167, though consistent expense coding on the general ledger remains an essential internal control to prevent audit disallowance.
Detailed Analysis of Non-Qualifying Expenditures and Exclusions
Indirect Research Costs and General and Administrative Overhead

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1) explicitly excludes indirect research expenditures and general and administrative (G&A) expenses from qualifying as in-house research expenses, even when such costs are incurred exclusively within or for the benefit of a dedicated research and development division. Both the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses (Section 4.b) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) establish that the functional use of an item in directly executing, supervising, or supporting qualified experimentation—not the departmental cost center or accounting label—governs whether an expenditure is direct or indirect.

In examination practice, this exclusion bars three recurring classes of overhead claims. First, general operational and administrative costs—including routine office supplies used by research engineers, researcher telephone and internet charges, travel, meals, entertainment, employee relocation costs, professional association dues, licensing or royalty payments, and general facility electricity, water, or natural gas—are ineligible.

Second, support functions lacking a direct experimental nexus are excluded under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3). Footnote 7 of the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) confirm that payroll personnel preparing salary checks for research scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, and corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters do not perform "direct support" of qualified research. However, tax practitioners must carefully distinguish general janitorial room cleaning from the specific regulatory example in Footnote 6 of the IRS ATG (codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)): a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research is engaged in qualified direct support. Consequently, specialized chemical solvents, calibration gases, or decontamination agents used by a laboratory technician to clean experimental reaction vessels between trial runs satisfy the direct nexus requirement and qualify as supply QREs, whereas floor wax and paper towels used by a janitor for general laboratory maintenance are excluded as G&A overhead.

Third, overhead loaded into self-constructed supplies is a primary target for IRS examination adjustments. Both the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses (Section 4.b) and the IRS Coordinated Issue Paper on Self-Constructed Assets (referenced in Chapter 10.a of the IRS ATG: Research Credit Issues) warn that taxpayers fabricating their own supplies, subassemblies, or tooling in-house frequently attempt to burden those "self-constructed supplies" with allocated facility depreciation, employee benefit overhead, travel, entertainment, and G&A costs. Only the direct, non-depreciable tangible materials incorporated into the item (along with separately reported qualified employee wages under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)) are eligible for the credit; all indirect overhead capitalized or allocated into self-constructed items must be stripped out.
Equipment, Capital Expenditures, and Leased Personal Property

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii), any tangible asset possessing a useful life extending beyond one year that is subject to wear, tear, exhaustion, or obsolescence in the taxpayer's business operations—such as a high-precision laser cutter, an industrial 3D printer, an oscilloscope, reusable production tooling retained by the taxpayer, or an environmental test chamber—constitutes a capital expenditure subject to the allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167 and cannot be claimed as a supply QRE.

Furthermore, taxpayers cannot circumvent the statutory depreciation bar by leasing or renting testing equipment rather than purchasing it outright. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4) (governing the use of personal property in taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985), amounts paid or incurred for the use or lease of personal property are explicitly disallowed as QREs, with the sole statutory exception of off-premises, third-party computer time-sharing under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4). In addition, the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses emphasizes that lease payments for equipment or facility assets represent payments for the intangible right to use property rather than acquisitions of tangible property, thereby failing the threshold statutory definition of a supply under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C).

body.text: Complex Scenarios: Pilot Models, Mixed-Use Materials, and Disposition
Pilot Models and the Process of Experimentation

In physical manufacturing, aerospace, automotive engineering, and life sciences, substantial material expenditures are incurred to design, fabricate, and test experimental models and trial production runs. A foundational point of regulatory precision—emphasized in Chapter 10.b.2 of the IRS ATG: Research Credit Issues (last updated June 8, 2026)—is that the word "prototype" does not appear anywhere in the relevant statutory provisions of IRC Section 41, IRC Section 174, or the corresponding Treasury Regulations. Instead, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4) (promulgated in Treasury Decision 9680 on July 21, 2014) governs experimental models under the defined legal term "pilot model". Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4), a "pilot model" is defined as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product, including a fully-functional representation or model of the product or, to the extent that the shrinking-back provisions of paragraph (a)(5) apply, a component of the product.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2), the research activity for which the pilot model is constructed must satisfy the statutory Four-Part Test applied separately to each business component. First, under the Section 174 Test codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), the expenditure must be paid or incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense—specifically, activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product or process. Second, under the Technological in Nature Test codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), the process of experimentation utilized to discover the information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science; pursuant to Treasury Decision 9104 (finalized in January 2004), the taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the broader field. Third, under the Business Component Test codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the taxpayer must intend that the information to be discovered be useful in the development of a new or improved business component, which is defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6), substantially all (80% or more) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation—identifying technical uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and systematically evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error—for a qualified purpose, namely a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, while excluding activities related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B).
Correction of the 80% Substantially-All Rule on Prototype Costs

A recurring technical error in R&D tax compliance is the assertion that if 80% or more ("substantially all") of the monetary costs incurred in building a prototype are attributable to a process of experimentation, the "Substantially-All Rule" permits the taxpayer to treat 100% of the prototype's material costs—including minor non-experimental commercial fabrication costs—as a qualified supply.

A rigorous examination of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) and specialized tax commentary demonstrates why that assertion is legally erroneous. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to the wage rule in § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in IRC § 41(d)(3). When 80% or more of the research activities for a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation, the Process of Experimentation test is satisfied even if the remaining 20% or less of the research activities do not constitute elements of a process of experimentation—provided, however, that those remaining research activities still satisfy the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (Section 174 eligibility) and are not otherwise excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4).

Consequently, non-experimental commercial production or fabrication costs can never be swept into supply QREs via the 80% rule. Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) (Production costs), costs paid or incurred in the actual production of a product after the elimination of technical uncertainty are categorically ineligible under IRC Section 174. Likewise, under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), any activity conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component is statutorily excluded from qualified research. Because the remaining ≤ 20% of activities under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) must still constitute eligible Section 174 research activities (§ 41(d)(1)(A)) and must not violate § 41(d)(4), post-uncertainty production or commercial fabrication costs remain strictly excluded. Furthermore, the 80% threshold measures research activities at the business-component level rather than 80% of a prototype's monetary purchase price, and satisfying the 80% activity test never relieves the taxpayer of the obligation to segregate eligible employee wages, non-depreciable supplies, and excluded production costs.

The regulatory examples codified in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(11) illustrate the mandatory segregation between pilot model costs and post-uncertainty production costs. In 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 3 (Custom Machine Pilot Model), manufacturer U enters into a contract to design and build a custom machine with uncertain design specifications, incurring $31,000 of total costs: $10,000 on materials and labor to produce a model used to evaluate and resolve the design uncertainty, plus $1,000 to test the model, followed by $20,000 to build the final machine for sale to the customer once design uncertainty has been eliminated. Under the regulation, only the $11,000 ($10,000 model fabrication plus $1,000 testing) qualifies under Section 174; the $20,000 production expenditure incurred after uncertainty was resolved is excluded under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2).

Similarly, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5) and (a)(11), Example 8 (Component-Level Shrinking-Back Pilot Model), demonstrates how the component rule restricts supply claims on large assemblies. In Example 8, aircraft engine manufacturer Y develops an experimental compressor blade (a pilot model component) and installs it on an existing commercial aircraft engine held in inventory to test fatigue performance. While Y's costs of producing and installing the experimental compressor blade qualify under Section 174, Y's underlying costs of producing the host aircraft engine on which the experimental blade was mounted do not qualify.
Disposition of Pilot Models and T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner

A historically contentious issue in IRS examinations was whether selling a prototype, pilot model, or experimental production mold to a customer—or using it in subsequent commercial operations—retroactively disqualified the material expenditures as supply QREs. The controlling judicial precedent on this question is T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner (also cited as TG Missouri Corporation v. Commissioner), 133 T.C. 278, Docket No. 8333-06, decided by the United States Tax Court on November 12, 2009.

In T.G. Missouri Corp., the taxpayer designed and manufactured injection-molded automotive components—including steering wheels, airbags, and body side molding—for original equipment manufacturers. Developing a production mold required 24 to 36 months of engineering design, iterative modification, and testing to satisfy customer specifications. TG Missouri contracted with third-party toolmakers to fabricate the steel molds according to TG Missouri's engineering designs and bore full financial risk unless and until the customer accepted sample parts produced from the mold. Where TG Missouri retained ownership of molds for its own internal manufacturing use, the company capitalized and depreciated them; however, for the molds at issue in tax years 1997, 1998, and 1999, TG Missouri sold the completed molds to its customers—transferring legal title and economic ownership to the customers while retaining physical possession solely to manufacture parts for those customers—and claimed the third-party tooling costs as supply QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).

During examination and subsequent litigation, the IRS disallowed the supply QREs under a "generic character" theory, arguing that because steel injection molds possess an inherent physical useful life extending beyond one year and experience wear and tear, they are inherently "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and IRC § 174(c) regardless of who holds economic ownership. The United States Tax Court rejected the IRS's "generic character" doctrine and its administrative "totally used or consumed" requirement, holding that whether property is "of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) must be determined specifically in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit by reference to IRC § 167. Because TG Missouri transferred ownership of the molds to its customers and held no depreciable economic interest in them, the molds were not subject to an allowance for depreciation in TG Missouri's hands and therefore qualified as supply QREs.

Following the Tax Court's decision in T.G. Missouri Corp., the Treasury Department issued proposed regulations in September 2013 (REG-124148-05) and finalized 26 CFR § 1.174-2 in July 2014 (T.D. 9680). Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and § 1.174-2(a)(11), Examples 5 and 7, the ultimate success, failure, sale, or internal demonstration use of a pilot model—even a $5,000,000 working experimental vertical-takeoff aircraft that is subsequently sold to a customer in a later year (Example 7)—does not disqualify the pre-production research and experimental expenditures under Section 174. However, for the tangible material costs of that pilot model to qualify as supplies under IRC Section 41, the pilot model must never be placed in service as a depreciable asset in the taxpayer's own hands under IRC § 167.
The table below details the governing legal treatment across the five primary pilot model and prototype disposition scenarios:

Non-Qualifying as Supply QRE (Eligible wages/contractors to design it may still qualify)
26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) & 26 CFR § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(2): Becomes depreciable property in taxpayer's hands under IRC § 167.
Must remove material costs from Section 41 supply QRE schedule; track design engineering wages separately under § 41(b)(2)(A)(i).

High Litigation Risk / Generally Disallowed if Normal Raw Material Inventory
Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner (applied in Stephens v. Commissioner) vs. T.G. Missouri: Raw materials that would have been purchased for COGS regardless of process R&D face IRS disallowance.
Isolate dedicated experimental test batches or scrap/waste directly attributable to trial runs rather than claiming bulk COGS raw materials.

body.text: Mixed-Use Materials and Mandatory Cost Allocation

When a taxpayer acquires bulk raw materials, chemical feedstocks, or electronic components that are used partly for qualified experimentation and partly for commercial manufacturing, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) mandate a strict proportional allocation. Only the exact fraction of the tangible material directly used in the process of experimentation prior to the elimination of technical uncertainty qualifies as a supply QRE.

Furthermore, tax practitioners must account for the sharp judicial distinction between product pilot models and process research conducted during commercial production runs, as established in the Tax Court jurisprudence comparing T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), and Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner (analyzed in Stephens v. Commissioner). Where raw materials constitute standard production inventory that the manufacturer would have purchased to manufacture commercial goods for sale regardless of whether an in-plant process experiment was conducted during that production run, the Tax Court in Union Carbide disallowed the raw material costs as supply QREs. By contrast, supplies purchased or requisitioned specifically to construct an experimental product or test an unproven design concept (as in T.G. Missouri) are eligible to the extent used to resolve technical uncertainty.
Worked Allocation Model: Mixed-Use Raw Material Batch

To illustrate the exact mechanics of mixed-use material allocation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1), and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2), consider the following hypothetical scenario involving Apex Medical Devices Inc. Assume Apex Medical Devices Inc. purchases a bulk lot of 1,000 titanium alloy housing blanks at a unit cost of $45.00 per blank, resulting in a total vendor invoice of $45,000.00 (1,000 units × $45.00). The engineering department requisitions 50 blanks from raw material inventory under Project Code RD-2026-04 to fabricate and stress-test three alternative wall-thickness geometries in order to resolve technical uncertainty regarding housing rupture pressure during autoclave sterilization, permanently altering or destroying all 50 blanks during cyclic pressure testing. Once the optimal wall-thickness geometry is validated and technical uncertainty is eliminated, the remaining 950 blanks are routed to commercial manufacturing to fulfill customer sales orders.
The step-by-step mathematical allocation proceeds as follows:

items: Qualified R&D Usage Ratio = 50 R&D Units ÷ 1,000 Total Units = 0.05 (or 5.0%)

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), only $2,250.00 qualifies as an eligible supply QRE, while the remaining $42,750.00 represents excluded commercial production cost (Cost of Goods Sold) under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2). To sustain the $2,250.00 supply QRE during an IRS examination, Apex Medical Devices Inc. must retain the $45,000.00 vendor invoice and purchase order, the Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) material requisition log documenting the transfer of 50 units from raw material inventory to the general ledger expense account R&D Consumables – Project RD-2026-04, and the autoclave stress-test engineering report documenting the evaluation and destruction of the 50 test units.
Special Regulatory Exception: Extraordinary Utilities
The General Utility Exclusion

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i), amounts paid or incurred for utilities—specifically water, electricity, and natural gas—used in a building in which qualified research is performed are treated as expenditures for general and administrative (G&A) expenses and are therefore excluded from QREs. By way of explicit illustration, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) states that amounts paid for electricity used for general laboratory lighting are treated as G&A expenses.
Qualifying Extraordinary Expenditures for Utilities

The sole regulatory exception to the general utility exclusion—and, as noted in Footnote 9 of the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses, the only exception to the general statutory rule restricting supplies to tangible property acquired by the taxpayer—is codified in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii). That provision states that to the extent the taxpayer can establish that the special character of the qualified research required additional extraordinary expenditures for utilities, those additional expenditures shall be treated as amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research.

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) illustrates this narrow carve-out by contrasting general laboratory lighting with amounts paid for electricity used in operating high-energy equipment for qualified research (such as laser or nuclear research), which may be treated as supply QREs to the extent the taxpayer establishes that the special character of the research demanded an extraordinary additional expenditure for electricity.

Chapter 10.b.2 of the IRS ATG: Research Credit Issues (last updated June 8, 2026) enforces a rigorous evidentiary standard for taxpayers claiming extraordinary utilities. The burden of proof rests entirely upon the taxpayer to substantiate both the extraordinary nature of the utility demand arising from the special character of the research and the exact incremental dollar expenditure above normal baseline facility consumption. Crucially, the IRS ATG instructs examiners that merely comparing the square-footage electricity usage in an administrative building with that of a research facility is insufficient to establish an extraordinary utility claim. Consequently, audit-ready claims require either direct utility sub-metering of the specific high-energy experimental apparatus (such as an experimental wind tunnel, particle accelerator, high-powered laser array, or specialized arc furnace) or a contemporaneous engineering load study that computes exact equipment kilowatt-hour draw multiplied by logged experimental run-hours and applicable utility tariff rates.
Financial Impact Analysis: Evaluating Supply QREs under Statutory Credit Formulas
Statutory Credit Mechanics and Marginal Return

While corporate tax planning models frequently estimate the net benefit of capturing qualified supplies by multiplying total QREs (Qualified Wages plus Qualified Supplies) by a simplified 6.5% effective credit rate (reflecting an industry CPA benchmark range of roughly 6% to 10% depending on the election method), tax directors evaluating the marginal return of segregating additional supply QREs must account for how the exact statutory formulas in 26 U.S.C. § 41(a) and § 41(c) operate on incremental expenditures.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c)(1)–(3) (the Regular Credit), the research credit equals 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's current-year QREs over the "base amount". The base amount is the product of the taxpayer's "fixed-base percentage" (capped at a statutory maximum of 16% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)) and the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the 4 preceding taxable years (§ 41(c)(1)), subject to a mandatory statutory floor under § 41(c)(2) stipulating that the base amount cannot be less than 50% of current-year QREs. Furthermore, under the statutory consistency rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A), QREs—including supply QREs—taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage for base years (taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989) must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the current credit year.

Alternatively, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) (the Alternative Simplified Credit, or ASC), at the election of the taxpayer, the research credit equals 14% of so much of the taxpayer's current-year QREs as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years. Under IRC § 280C(c)(3) (Section 280C Coordination), a taxpayer must either reduce its otherwise allowable Section 174 deduction or amortization by the full amount of the gross research credit claimed, or make a timely election on its original tax return under IRC § 280C(c)(3) to claim a reduced credit.

Evaluating the statutory mechanics reveals an important second-order financial effect regarding incremental supply QREs. Once a taxpayer's qualified employee wages already exceed its current-year statutory base amount (for example, 50% of the prior 3-year average QREs under the ASC), every additional $1.00 of properly substantiated supply QREs added in the current year increases the gross ASC by a full 14.0% ($0.14 per dollar) in that taxable year—or up to 20.0% ($0.20 per dollar) under the Regular Credit if the taxpayer is not constrained by the 50% minimum base floor—while moderately increasing the 3-year rolling base calculation for the subsequent three taxable years.
Worked Financial Comparison: Statutory ASC vs. Simplified Effective Rate Benchmark

To demonstrate the divergence between a simplified effective rate approximation (6.5%) and the exact statutory Alternative Simplified Credit formula under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A), consider the following hypothetical calculation for Precision Robotics Corp. Assume Precision Robotics Corp. recorded total QREs in the prior 3 taxable years of $480,000.00 (Year −3), $500,000.00 (Year −2), and $520,000.00 (Year −1). In the current taxable year, Precision Robotics Corp. incurs $500,000.00 in qualified employee wages under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and identifies $125,000.00 in qualified supply expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) for non-depreciable alloy stock, optical sensors, and printed circuit boards consumed in fabricating and destructively testing experimental robotic actuators, bringing combined current-year QREs to $625,000.00 (with supplies representing 20.0% of total QREs).

body.text: Documentation, Form 6765 Reporting, and Audit Defense
The Recordkeeping Standard and IRS Examination Posture

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), any taxpayer claiming a research credit under IRC Section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit, operating in tandem with the general federal tax record-retention rules under 26 CFR § 1.6001-1.

When auditing supply claims, IRS examiners execute two primary directives established in the IRS Audit Techniques Guides (Qualified Research Expenses and Research Credit Issues). First, with respect to substantial supply proportions, Section 4.b of the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses (updated July 2, 2026) explicitly instructs IRS examiners that supply QREs, in general, should represent a small portion of total QREs, and that when claimed supply QREs are substantial, examiners must be alerted to the possible inclusion of capital assets or other ineligible expenses being claimed as QREs. Second, with respect to cost accounting system audits, under Chapter 10.c.2 of the IRS ATG: Research Credit Issues (updated June 8, 2026), examiners are directed to document the taxpayer's cost accounting system in granular detail, evaluate how project records are maintained, and issue formal Notices of Proposed Adjustment (or administrative summonses if material records are withheld) whenever substantiation is unreliable, insufficient, or lacks a verifiable project-level nexus.
Project-Level Reporting on Redesigned Form 6765
The IRS enforces specific disclosure of qualified supply expenses through two procedural channels: original returns filing the redesigned Form 6765, and amended returns or claims for refund.

On original tax returns utilizing the redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) and the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), the IRS has institutionalized upfront, business-component-level expenditure reporting across Section F and Section G. In Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), filers must report "Total costs of supplies for all business components" on Line 43 (which carries over from Section G, Column 54 if Section G is completed), alongside total qualified wages on Line 42, computer rental or lease costs on Line 44, contract research expenses on Line 45, and total QREs on Line 48. Controlled group members filing separate tax returns must report only their own standalone qualified supply expenses on Line 43, rather than the combined controlled group supply QREs.

In Section G (Business Component Information), filers must report each individual business component generating QREs up to the 80% of total QREs / Top 50 business components threshold, aggregating any remaining smaller projects under the "Aggregate Business Components" entry in Column 49(c). For each listed business component, the taxpayer must report in Columns 49(a)–(e) the entity Employer Identification Number (EIN), the Principal Business Activity (PBA) code, the Business Component Name or Unique Alphanumeric Identifier (matching internal books and records), the Business Component Type (1. Product, 2. Process, or 3. All Others), and the Software category if applicable. Crucially, in Column 54 (Cost of supplies), the taxpayer must enter the exact dollar expenditure for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research for that specific business component. Under the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), completion of Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless the taxpayer is filing an amended return claiming or increasing a research credit) and is mandatory for all filers for tax years beginning after 2025 (subject to small-taxpayer Section G exemptions and ASC 730 Directive rules).

For amended returns and claims for refund—governed by IRS administrative guidance updated September 27, 2026, and October 1, 2026, following the October 15, 2021 Chief Counsel Memorandum (IR-2021-203) and the June 18, 2024 modification (with the transition period permitting 45 days to perfect a deficient claim via Letter 6426C or Letter 6428 extended through January 10, 2027)—any taxpayer filing an amended return or Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR) that includes a Section 41 refund claim must provide three mandatory items of information at the time of filing. First, the taxpayer must identify all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that taxable year. Second, the taxpayer must identify all research activities performed for each business component and, when utilizing redesigned Form 6765, complete Column 49(f) describing the information sought to be discovered, which is mandatory only for amended returns or AARs claiming or increasing a Section 41 credit. Third, the taxpayer must provide a breakdown of the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year, a requirement that may be satisfied by submitting a completed Form 6765.

For refund claims postmarked or submitted on or after June 18, 2024, the IRS waived the requirement to provide at initial filing the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the specific information each individual sought to discover, although IRS examiners retain full authority to request both items if the refund claim is selected for examination.
Four-Pillar Supplies Substantiation Checklist

To satisfy the recordkeeping mandate of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), support Form 6765 Section G (Column 54) disclosures, and withstand IRS examination scrutiny, corporate taxpayers must maintain a four-pillar audit trail for every claimed supply expenditure:

cells: 1. Transactional Financial Records
Itemized vendor invoices, purchase orders (POs), payment receipts, and bills of lading.
Substantiates that the expenditure was "paid or incurred" during the taxable year and verifies the tangible nature of the item under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) & (C).
2. General Ledger & Fixed-Asset Reconciliation
Chart of accounts, General Ledger (GL) detail, project cost codes, and fixed-asset/depreciation schedules.
Confirms that claimed supplies were expensed rather than capitalized and depreciated under IRC § 167, preventing double-dipping and satisfying 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii).
3. Technical & Project Nexus Records
Engineering bills of materials (BOMs), lab notebooks, CAD designs, test plans, destructive test logs, QA reports, and Section G Column 49(c) project identifiers.
Proves the supply was directly used by qualified personnel in performing "qualified services" (26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)) within a process of experimentation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)).
4. Allocation & Exception Workpapers
Inventory check-out/requisition logs, pilot model disposition contracts, and sub-metered engineering studies for extraordinary utilities.
Substantiates mixed-use R&D vs. COGS splits (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2)), non-depreciable customer ownership (T.G. Missouri, 133 T.C. 278), or extraordinary utilities (26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii)).

body.text: Comprehensive Legal Verification Audit Matrix
The following verification matrix synthesizes the statutory, regulatory, judicial, and administrative audit conclusions across all seventeen core compliance claims governing IRC Section 41 supplies:

cells: Supplies represent a core statutory category of QREs under IRC Section 41 alongside employee wages, computer time-sharing, and contract research expenses.
Verified

Confirmed. Section 41(b)(1) defines QREs as (A) in-house research expenses—comprising wages (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), supplies (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), and right to use computers (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(iii))—plus (B) contract research expenses (§ 41(b)(3)).
26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) includes any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research as an in-house research expense.
Verified
Confirmed verbatim for § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), while § 41(b)(2)(C) provides the statutory definition of the term "supplies".
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2 stipulates that a qualified supply must constitute "tangible personal property" and imposes the land and depreciation exclusions.
Corrected
26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(i)–(ii); 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b); IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses

The tangibility requirement and the exclusions for (i) land or improvements to land and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation are codified directly in the statute at 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), using the exact phrase "any tangible property".
Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), supplies must be used in the performance of "qualified services" conducted by an employee of the taxpayer or a person acting in a similar capacity.
Verified
Confirmed verbatim in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1), which applies § 41(b)(2)(B) "without regard to the last sentence thereof," barring the 80% employee wage rule from carrying over to supplies.
Only materials physically consumed or destroyed are eligible, and financial accounting expensing is a direct determinant of tax eligibility.
Corrected
T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009); 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1); IRS ATG

In T.G. Missouri Corp., the Tax Court rejected the IRS's "totally used or consumed" doctrine, holding that the statutory test is whether property is subject to depreciation under IRC § 167 in the hands of the taxpayer; legal depreciability governs over bookkeeping labels.
Supplies frequently constitute 15%–20% of QREs in manufacturing alongside wages (~70%) and contractors (~10%–15%).
Corrected
IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses (Section 4.b, updated July 2, 2026)

While 15%–20% is an illustrative consultancy estimate for hardware-heavy industries, the IRS ATG explicitly instructs examiners that supply QREs "in general, should represent a small portion of total QREs" and that substantial supply claims warrant audit scrutiny.
Depreciation itself is never considered a QRE under IRC Section 41.
Verified
IRS ATG: Qualified Research Activities (Section 2, updated July 2, 2026); 26 CFR § 1.174-2(b)(1)
Confirmed. While depreciation allowances on research equipment may in certain cases be treated as Section 174 expenses under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(b)(1), depreciation is never a QRE under IRC Section 41.

Indirect research expenditures and G&A expenses—including travel, meals, telephone, relocation, dues, royalties, license fees, general janitorial cleaning, and accounting for research expenses—are excluded.
Verified

Confirmed. While general lab cleaning by a janitor or accounting for research expenses is excluded G&A, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research or a machinist machining a part for an experimental model performs qualified direct support.
Rental or lease costs of testing equipment or facility space are excluded from supplies QREs, whereas off-premises computer time-sharing is permitted under specific rules.
Verified

Confirmed. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4), amounts paid for the use of personal property are disallowed except for off-premises, non-taxpayer-operated computer time-sharing where the taxpayer is not the primary user.
The IRS cautions that "Taxpayer labels are not controlling" when evaluating whether an expenditure qualifies as a supply or prototype QRE.
Verified
IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses (Section 4.b) & Research Credit Issues (Chapter 10.b.2)

Confirmed verbatim in both IRS Audit Techniques Guides, which also note that the word "prototype" does not appear in the Code or Treasury Regulations (which instead define "pilot model" in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4)).

Under the "Substantially-All Rule," if 80% or more of the total monetary costs incurred in building a prototype are attributed to experimentation, 100% of the prototype materials (including minor non-experimental production costs) qualify as supplies.
Corrected

26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) applies the 80% threshold to research activities for a business component, not to 80% of a prototype's monetary cost, and requires that any remaining ≤ 20% activities still satisfy § 41(d)(1)(A) (Section 174 eligibility) and not violate § 41(d)(4); post-uncertainty production costs are barred under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2).

The ultimate success, failure, or eventual sale of a pilot model does not preclude material costs from qualifying if incurred to resolve technical uncertainty and not depreciable in the taxpayer's hands.
Verified
Confirmed in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) ("The ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product is not relevant to a determination of eligibility under section 174") and Examples 5 and 7.
United States Tax Court precedent confirmed that molds purchased by a taxpayer, researched upon, and sold to a customer were qualified supplies eligible for the research credit.
Corrected
T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278, Docket No. 8333-06 (U.S. Tax Ct., Nov. 12, 2009)

Verified with complete official citation (T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278, Docket No. 8333-06, decided November 12, 2009) and exact holding for tax years 1997–1999 regarding non-depreciability in the hands of the taxpayer under IRC § 167 and § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii).
Mixed-use materials used for both R&D and commercial production must be allocated so that only the portion directly tied to experimentation is claimed.
Verified
26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1); 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2); Union Carbide Corp. vs. T.G. Missouri Corp.
Confirmed, incorporating the judicial distinction from Union Carbide Corp. regarding the disallowance risk of claiming standard COGS raw material inventory in commercial plant process research.

General utilities (water, electricity, gas, general lab lighting) are excluded as G&A, but "extraordinary utilities" required by the special character of qualified research qualify as supplies under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii).
Verified
26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i)–(ii); IRS ATG: Research Credit Issues (Chapter 10.b.2, updated June 8, 2026)

Confirmed verbatim in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i)–(ii), subject to the explicit IRS ATG rule that comparing square-footage electricity usage between an administrative building and a research facility is insufficient.
Taxpayers are required to disclose total and business-component qualified supply expenses claimed for the year on IRS filings and refund claims.
Verified
Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2024); Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2025); IRS Refund Claim Guidance (updated Sept./Oct. 2026)

Confirmed. Form 6765 requires reporting total supplies on Section F (Line 43) and business-component supplies on Section G (Column 54) (optional pre-2026 except amended returns; mandatory post-2025), alongside valid refund claim rules (45-day perfection period extended through Jan. 10, 2027).
Contract research is 65% allowable by default, and simplified models estimate financial impact at a 6.5% effective rate compared to the statutory credit formulas.

26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), § 41(b)(3)(A)–(D), & § 41(c)(4)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1)

body.text: Strategic Compliance Governance and Actionable Protocols

Integrating the statutory mandates of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and the regulatory directives of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b) and § 1.174-2 with IRS examination standards yields five concrete governance protocols for corporate tax departments, engineering leaders, and accounting teams.

First, corporate tax and accounting departments should establish a codified R&D supplies classification matrix across procurement and financial accounting. Organizations must implement a formal internal accounting policy mapping raw material inventory items, laboratory consumables, custom tooling, and pilot model components against the statutory gates of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1). This internal policy must proactively segregate depreciable capital equipment governed by IRC § 167, leased personal property disallowed under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4), software licenses, patent attorney fees, and indirect overhead from R&D supply general ledger accounts prior to tax return preparation.

Second, enterprises must align ERP project coding directly with Form 6765 Section G business components. Because Section G of redesigned Form 6765 requires reporting "Cost of supplies" (Column 54) by unique business component alphanumeric identifier (Column 49(c)) for tax years beginning after 2025 and on all amended returns claiming or increasing a research credit, taxpayers can no longer rely on lump-sum year-end estimates extracted from generic general ledger "Materials" or "Cost of Goods Sold" accounts. Purchase orders and ERP inventory requisitions must enforce mandatory Business Component and Project Code tagging at the exact point of material check-out.

Third, physical manufacturers should institute a formal pilot model and custom tooling accounting review protocol. For manufacturers fabricating pilot models under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4) or customer-ordered production tooling governed by T.G. Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), tax and fixed-asset accounting teams must review customer contracts and capital asset ledgers concurrently. Teams must verify that only design, fabrication, and testing costs incurred prior to the elimination of technical uncertainty are captured in accordance with 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2), avoiding any reliance on the misconception that the 80% activity rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) sweeps in post-uncertainty commercial production costs. Concurrently, accounting personnel must verify whether the resulting pilot model or mold is scrapped, sold to the customer without taxpayer depreciation, or retained as internal depreciable tooling under IRC § 167.

Fourth, facilities and tax engineering teams must deploy sub-metering or engineering baseline studies before claiming extraordinary utilities. Because Chapter 10.b.2 of the IRS ATG: Research Credit Issues explicitly rejects square-footage electricity comparisons between administrative and R&D buildings, taxpayers operating high-energy research equipment should install dedicated utility sub-meters or commission contemporaneous engineering load studies to isolate extraordinary utility consumption under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii).

Fifth, corporate tax departments should prepare contemporaneous tax position memoranda for high-scrutiny supply categories. Whenever claimed supply QREs constitute a substantial percentage of total QREs—triggering the examination alert in Section 4.b of the IRS ATG: Qualified Research Expenses—or involve mixed-use inventory allocations or customer-sold pilot models, tax counsel and internal auditors should assemble a pre-filing Tax Position Memorandum linking the transactional vendor invoices, general ledger entries, engineering bills of materials, customer contracts, and controlling legal authorities.
